claim: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific literature and consensus in the field.

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
source: Visual speed is believed to be underestimated at low contrast, which has been proposed as an explanation of excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from prior research literature.

claim: Speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
source: we confirm that speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene independently of their distance from the viewer.
evidence: This claim is confirmed by experimental data from the study's psychophysics measurements and driving simulation.

claim: When contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Speed overestimation in fog prompts drivers to decelerate.
source: However, we show that when contrast is reduced more for distant objects, as is the case in real fog, visual speed is actually overestimated, prompting drivers to decelerate.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the driving simulation experiments.

claim: Perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
source: we demonstrate for the first time that perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast over the visual scene rather than the global level of contrast per se.
evidence: This claim is demonstrated through experimental data comparing fog and anti-fog conditions with identical global contrast.

claim: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background.
source: Visual contrast is usually referred to as the difference in brightness between an object and the background (Hofstetter et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Classical vision research experiments systematically investigated how visual contrast affects objects motion perception.
source: Classical vision research experiments systematically investigated how visual contrast affects objects motion perception (Thompson, 1982; Stone and Thompson, 1992; Blakemore and Snowden, 1999; Anstis, 2003).

claim: The perceived speed of two-dimensional moving objects is underestimated when visual contrast is reduced.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classical vision research studies.

claim: The underestimation of visual speed at low contrast applies also to perceived self-motion in three-dimensional environments.

claim: Speed underestimation at low contrast was proposed as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
source: This finding was proposed—and is still considered—as a possible explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from prior research literature.

claim: In all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.
source: In the abovementioned studies, and more generally in all studies having assessed the effect of visual contrast on motion perception, contrast was reduced uniformly for all objects of the visual scene, irrespective of their distance from the observer.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.

claim: Uniform contrast reduction is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.
source: While uniform contrast reduction is a valid model to assess the perception of two-dimensional patterns moving on a computer screen, it is a poor model to investigate how an atmospheric phenomenon like fog affects motion perception in three-dimensional environments.

claim: The contrast of the visual scene decreases with distance in fog.

claim: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
source: When visibility is better in the peripheral than in the central visual field, as is the case in fog, speed is overestimated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the fog conditions.

claim: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog and thereby obscuring more the peripheral than the central region of the visual field, inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
source: Inverting the direction of the contrast gradient with anti-fog and thereby obscuring more the peripheral than the central region of the visual field, inverts the perceptual bias such that speed is now underestimated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the anti-fog conditions.

claim: The visibility gradient plays a critical role in perceived speed.
source: This highlights the critical role of the visibility gradient in perceived speed, explaining why speed is unexpectedly overestimated in fog despite a global reduction of visibility.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results comparing fog and anti-fog.

claim: There is a direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.
source: Importantly, our results also evidence the direct relationship between perceived and produced speed.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results showing consistent patterns across perception and behavior experiments.

claim: Speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower.
source: Specifically, speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower, whereas speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the driving experiments.

claim: Speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
source: Specifically, speed overestimation systematically prompted drivers to drive slower, whereas speed underestimation led to faster driving paces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the driving experiments.

claim: Driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
source: This demonstrates that driving speed is strongly affected by perceived visual speed.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results showing consistent patterns across perception and behavior experiments.

claim: In 'real-life' driving, the roadsides usually include various objects and landmarks as trees, buildings, traffic signs, or pedestrians.
source: In 'real-life' driving, the roadsides usually include various objects and landmarks as trees, buildings, traffic signs, or pedestrians.
evidence: This claim is based on common knowledge about real-world driving environments.

claim: Objects next to the road can have a cognitive influence on driving speed because they constitute potential obstacles that increase the risk of collision.
source: Such objects next to the road can have a cognitive influence on driving speed because they constitute potential obstacles that increase the risk of collision (e.g., tree or building if one drives out of the road and cars or pedestrians suddenly crossing the road).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about cognitive factors in driving.

claim: The roadsides of the driving scenario consisted of a grass texture clear of any object and landmark.
source: Therefore, the roadsides of our driving scenario consisted of a grass texture clear of any object and landmark.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: The design prevented cognitive factors from biasing the results.
source: This prevented cognitive factors as those mentioned above to bias our results, but importantly, it also prevented subjects of using these landmarks to estimate moving speed.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the purpose of the experimental design.

claim: Adding landmarks or other 'higher-level' cues would have given the subjects the possibility to use some cognitive strategies to estimate speed.
source: Indeed, adding landmarks or other 'higher-level' cues would have given the subjects the possibility to use some cognitive strategies to estimate speed.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about alternative experimental designs.

claim: Subjects could have used relative size information of landmarks to infer distances and counted passing them to assess speed.
source: For instance, subjects could have used relative size information of landmarks to infer distances and counted passing them to assess speed.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential cognitive strategies.

claim: At a 'pure' perceptual level, objects next to the road can also contribute to increase peripheral visual flow, thereby altering perceived speed.
source: Yet, one could argue that at a 'pure' perceptual level, objects next to the road can also contribute to increase peripheral visual flow, thereby altering perceived speed.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential perceptual effects.

claim: The scene used consisted of a rough asphalt pavement and roughly textured grass roadsides.
source: However, the scene we used consisted of a rough asphalt pavement and roughly textured grass roadsides (see Figure 2).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rough textures provided participants with rich visual flow information when driving.
source: These rough textures provided participants with rich visual flow information when driving, as attested by our results.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: In the 'clear visibility' condition, participants estimated visual speed with great accuracy.
source: Specifically, in the 'clear visibility' condition, participants estimated visual speed with great accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the clear visibility condition.

claim: The variability of speed estimates was small (i.e., low JNDs) in all conditions, and even more with clear visibility.
source: In addition, the variability of speed estimates was small (i.e., low JNDs) in all conditions, and even more with clear visibility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on JNDs.

claim: The driving scenario provided robust visual flow information allowing for reliable speed estimates.
source: Those elements indicate that our driving scenario provided robust visual flow information allowing for reliable speed estimates.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results showing accurate speed estimates.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the primary visual cortex.
source: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported at early stages of visual processing, as the retina (Shapley and Victor, 1978), the lateral geniculate nucleus (Solomon et al., 2002), and the primary visual cortex (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Polat et al., 1998; Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Contrast-dependent modulation of neural activity has been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5).
source: It has also been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008) and speed detection (Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983b), notably via feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area (Maunsell and van Essen, 1983a; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: The middle temporal area (MT or V5) plays an important role in motion processing.
source: It has also been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008) and speed detection (Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983b), notably via feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area (Maunsell and van Essen, 1983a; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: The middle temporal area (MT or V5) plays an important role in speed detection.
source: It has also been reported in the middle temporal area (MT or V5), an area playing an important role in motion processing (Pack et al., 2005; Bartels et al., 2008) and speed detection (Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983b), notably via feedforward projections to the medial superior temporal area (Maunsell and van Essen, 1983a; Ungerleider and Desimone, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological research.

claim: Linking neurophysiological findings with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
source: Yet, linking these neurophysiological findings with the effect of contrast on perceived speed in humans is not straightforward.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the complexity of relating neural and perceptual findings.

claim: The observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.
source: For instance, the observation that MT neurons tuned to high speeds are strongly activated by slow stimuli at low contrast (Pack et al., 2005) would predict speed overestimation at low contrast.
evidence: This claim is an inference from cited neurophysiological findings.

claim: The prediction of speed overestimation from MT neuron activity is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction.
source: This is the opposite of what has been usually observed with uniform contrast reduction, including in the current study.
evidence: This claim is an inference comparing neurophysiological predictions with behavioral data.

claim: The inconsistency between MT neuron activity and behavioral observations might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
source: As stated by Pack et al. (2005), this inconsistency might be resolved by assuming a bias towards slow speeds when the total MT population activity is low.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: A bias towards slow speed is precisely what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception.
source: Such a bias towards slow speed is precisely what is proposed by Bayesian models of speed perception (Weiss et al., 2002; Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy.
source: Specifically, these models rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy, and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence: This claim describes the assumptions of Bayesian models from cited literature.

claim: Bayesian models assume that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
source: Specifically, these models rely on the assumption that speed 'measurements' are intrinsically noisy, and that based on our everyday experience, slower motions are more likely to occur than faster ones—resulting in an elevated prior for slow speeds.
evidence: This claim describes the assumptions of Bayesian models from cited literature.

claim: Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast.
source: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical literature.

claim: Speed overestimation observed at higher speeds is more difficult for Bayesian models to account for.
source: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical literature.

claim: Speed overestimation observed at low luminance is more difficult for Bayesian models to account for.
source: Whereas Bayesian models of speed perception can accurately predict speed underestimation at low contrast (Stocker and Simoncelli, 2006), speed overestimation observed at higher speeds (Thompson et al., 2006) and at low luminance (Hammett et al., 2007) are more difficult to account for.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical literature.

claim: Alternative models have proposed that speed is encoded as 'the ratio of the responses of physiologically plausible temporal filters'.
source: Alternative models have proposed that speed is encoded as 'the ratio of the responses of physiologically plausible temporal filters' (Hammett et al., 2000; Hammett et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to alternative theoretical models.

claim: 'Ratio models' account for both under- and overestimation of speed at low contrast.
source: These 'ratio models' account for both under- and overestimation of speed at low contrast (Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to theoretical literature.

claim: None of the abovementioned models addressed situations in which the amount of contrast reduction differed for different areas of the moving visual scene, as is the case when driving in fog.
source: However, none of the abovementioned models addressed situations in which the amount of contrast reduction differed for different areas of the moving visual scene, as is the case when driving in fog.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the limitations of existing models based on the current experimental findings.

claim: Existing models do not explain the differences in speed perception observed with uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.
source: In that respect, these models do not explain the differences in speed perception observed here with uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the limitations of existing models based on the current experimental findings.

claim: Existing models do not account for opposite biases evoked with the same global contrast reduction at the same actual speed.
source: They do not account for opposite biases evoked with the same global contrast reduction at the same actual speed.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the limitations of existing models based on the current experimental findings.

claim: Poor visibility conditions affect millions of drivers around the world.
source: Poor visibility conditions affect millions of drivers around the world.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about driving conditions.

claim: Thousands of drivers die each year in a car accident.
source: Thousands of them die each year in a car accident.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about traffic safety statistics.

claim: Excessive speed constitutes a major causal factor for car accidents.
source: Excessive speed constitutes a major causal factor for these car accidents.
evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about traffic safety.

claim: Contrarily to what was previously believed, speed is overestimated in fog because visibility is poorer in the central than in the peripheral area of the visual field.
source: In particular, we show that contrarily to what was previously believed, speed is overestimated in fog because visibility is poorer in the central than in the peripheral area of the visual field.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The behavioural consequence of speed overestimation in fog is a natural tendency to drive at a slower pace.
source: We also show that the behavioural consequence of this speed overestimation is a natural tendency to drive at a slower pace.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the driving experiments.

claim: Drivers should probably listen to their visual system when it prompts them to decelerate.
source: Therefore, drivers should probably listen to their visual system when it prompts them to decelerate.
evidence: This claim is a recommendation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Thirty-two experienced drivers (23 males and 9 females; aged 21–35 years, mean = 25.3 years) participated voluntarily in the study.
source: Thirty-two experienced drivers (23 males and 9 females; aged 21–35 years, mean = 25.3 years) participated voluntarily in the study (12 in experiment 1, 10 in experiment 2, and 10 in experiments 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim describes the participant demographics.

claim: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This claim describes the participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Participants were paid, naive as to the purpose of the research, and gave their informed consent before taking part in the experiment.
source: They were paid, naive as to the purpose of the research, and gave their informed consent before taking part in the experiment.
evidence: This claim describes the ethical procedures of the study.

claim: The study was performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was performed in accordance with the ethical standards laid down in the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki, in line with Max Planck Society policy and in compliance with all relevant German legislation.
evidence: This claim describes the ethical standards followed in the study.

claim: All experiments were performed in an immersive virtual environment.
source: All experiments were performed in an immersive virtual environment.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: The participants were seated in a simplified vehicle mock-up equipped with steering wheel and pedals.
source: For all experiments, the participants were seated in a simplified vehicle mock-up equipped with steering wheel and pedals.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: The steering wheel haptic feedback was disabled so that no speed information could be inferred from the wheel feedback.
source: The steering wheel haptic feedback was disabled so that no speed information could be inferred from the wheel feedback.
evidence: This claim describes an experimental control.

claim: The mock-up was located at the centre of a large semi-spherical screen equipped with a multi-projection system.
source: The mock-up was located at the centre of a large semi-spherical screen equipped with a multi-projection system.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental setup.

claim: A cylindrical screen with a curved extension onto the floor provided a projection surface of 230° (horizontally) × 125° (vertically).
source: More specifically, a cylindrical screen with a curved extension onto the floor provided a projection surface of 230° (horizontally) × 125° (vertically).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental setup specifications.

claim: The resulting surface was entirely covered by four LCD projectors, with a resolution of 1400 × 1050 pixels each.
source: The resulting surface was entirely covered by four LCD projectors, with a resolution of 1400 × 1050 pixels each.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental setup specifications.

claim: The visual stimulus consisted of a virtual environment where a textured plane reproducing a straight single-lane road was scrolled at different speeds.
source: The visual stimulus consisted of a virtual environment where a textured plane reproducing a straight single-lane road was scrolled at different speeds.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: For the distance-dependent contrast reduction, the blending factor was determined by e−f·d, where f is the density of the fog and d is the distance from the observer to the depicted object.
source: For the distance-dependent contrast reduction, the blending factor was determined by e−f·d, where f is the density of the fog and d is the distance from the observer to the depicted object.
evidence: This claim describes the technical implementation of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The fog density value was set to 0.1 for the medium visibility condition and 0.3 for the poor condition.
source: We set the fog density value to 0.1 for the medium visibility condition and 0.3 for the poor condition, in a range from 0 (full visibility) to 1 (no visibility).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental parameters.

claim: The fog density values correspond to a meteorological visibility range (MVR) of 30 and 10 m, respectively.
source: These values correspond to a meteorological visibility range (MVR) of 30 and 10 m, respectively.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental parameters in real-world terms.

claim: The MVR indicates the distance at which a white object appears with a 5% contrast.
source: The MVR indicates the distance at which a white object appears with a 5% contrast (Kovalev and Eichinger, 2004).
evidence: This claim defines a technical term with citation support.

claim: For the 2IFC procedure used in experiments 1 and 3, 80 trials per condition were performed.
source: For the two-interval forced-choice (2IFC) procedure used in experiments 1 and 3, 80 trials per condition were performed, for a total of 1200 randomly interleaved trials in experiment 1 (two sessions of six blocks each, total duration of 2.5 hr) and 240 in experiment 3 (two blocks, total duration of 30 min).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.

claim: For experiments 2 and 4, each subject performed five trials per condition.
source: For experiments 2 and 4, each subject performed five trials per condition, and mean driving speed was computed for each subject and condition.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design.
